result: Bicuculline injections at various pFL sites (−0.2 mm to +0.8 mm from VIIc) consistently elicited ABD recruitment, but the response strength, duration, and onset varied along the rostro-caudal axis. The most robust and enduring changes in tidal volume, minute ventilation, and combined respiratory responses occurred at more rostral pFL locations (+0.6/+0.8 mm from VIIc), with the +0.6 mm location showing the fastest response onset.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states the study presents 'solid evidence for a valuable finding of pharmacological mapping' and addresses 'where these regions lie anatomically.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'convincingly show that although bicuculline injections at all coordinates of the pFL generated an expiratory response, the most rostral locations...play the strongest role in generating active expiration.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the data provide novel insights into the importance of rostral locations in controlling active expiration.'

result: Multivariate analysis of the respiratory cycle differentiated between locations, revealing distinct features including late-E 'tails', inspiratory 'bulbs', and post-I 'feet'. The strongest deformations of the respiratory loop during late-E and post-I occurred with injections at +0.8 mm, while injections at +0.6 mm produced more pronounced deformations during the inspiratory phase. This novel analytical approach enabled more precise assessment of how targeted stimulation affects particular phases of the respiratory cycle.
evaluation: Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly praise the novel analytical methods. Reviewer 2 states 'Major strengths of this work include...the use of a novel phase-plane analysis' and notes the authors 'construct a comprehensive functional map revealing functional nuances in respiratory responses.' Reviewer 3 emphasizes 'The authors use innovative analytic methods to characterize the respiratory effects of bicuculline injections into various areas of the pFL.' No concerns are raised about the validity of these analytical approaches.

result: Histological analysis confirmed that injection sites were positioned ventrolateral to the facial nucleus with no overlap between fluorobead-marked injection sites and PHOX2B+ cells in the RTN, or with TH+ cells in C1/A5 areas. Bicuculline specifically activated disinhibited cells within ~300 μm of injection sites and did not activate PHOX2B+ cells beyond baseline levels, particularly at rostral locations (+0.1 mm and beyond).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms this finding: 'The authors also confirmed histologically that none of the injection sites overlapped grossly with PHOX2B+ neurons, thus confirming the specificity of the injections in the pFL and not the neighboring RTN.' This anatomical confirmation is treated as an important validation of the experimental approach, with no concerns raised about the histological methods or interpretations.

result: The elicited ABD response was characterized by a late-E component in the ∫ABD EMG trace and a downward deflection in airflow signifying active expiration across all experimental groups. In the most rostral groups (+0.6 mm and +0.8 mm), the ∫ABD EMG traces exhibited a tonic expiratory component preceding the late-E peak. Area under the curve (AUC) analysis revealed that airflow was substantially altered in all three phases of the respiratory cycle, with effects strongest when targeting rostral areas of the pFL.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states the authors 'convincingly show' that responses at rostral locations 'were characterized by a strong impact on the duration and strength of ABD activation.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'The data provide novel insights into the importance of rostral locations in controlling active expiration.' The detailed characterization of ABD responses across respiratory phases is not questioned by any reviewer.

result: Bicuculline injection induced changes in respiratory parameters including frequency, tidal volume (VT), minute ventilation (VE), and oxygen consumption (VO2). The drop in respiratory frequency was significant only in the two most caudal groups. VT increased in all locations except −0.2 mm, with the peak at +0.6 mm. VE increased at rostral locations but decreased at the most caudal location. VO2 dropped only at the most rostral sites (+0.6 mm and +0.8 mm), and the VE/VO2 ratio increased only at these two rostral locations, suggesting hyperventilation.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes that responses at rostral locations were 'characterized by...a robust change in tidal volume and minute ventilation,' explicitly affirming these findings. Reviewer 3 confirms 'The results indicate that injections at more rostral pFL locations induce the most robust changes in tidal volume, minute ventilation, and combined respiratory responses.' No reviewer questions the validity of these respiratory parameter measurements or their interpretation.

result: Responses had shorter duration in the most caudal locations (−0.2 mm; +0.1 mm; +0.4 mm) compared to rostral locations (+0.6 mm; +0.8 mm). The ABD response initiated following the second bicuculline injection in all groups except at +0.6 mm, where it commenced following the first injection. The coupling of ∫ABD EMG and ∫DIA EMG peak signals was notably weaker at the most caudal location compared to rostral groups.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms that rostral location responses were 'characterized by a strong impact on the duration and strength of ABD activation.' The temporal dynamics and coupling measurements are part of the comprehensive characterization that reviewers praise, with no concerns raised about these specific findings.

result: Bicuculline has previously been shown to exhibit inhibitory effects on Ca2+-activated K+ currents and induce nonspecific potentiation of NMDA currents. Therefore, activation of late-E neurons and active expiration may be triggered by secondary pharmacological effects of bicuculline beyond GABAergic disinhibition.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges this limitation: 'Although a caveat of the approach is that bicuculine injections have indiscriminate effects on other neuronal populations in the region (GABAergic, glycinergic, and glutamatergic), the results can largely be interpreted as modulation of neuronal populations in different regions of the pFL have differential effects on expiratory output. This limitation of the pharmacological approach has also been aptly discussed by the authors.' Reviewer 3 similarly notes 'Bicuculline injections increase the excitability of neurons. Aside of blocking GABA receptors, bicuculline also inhibits calcium-activated potassium currents and potentiates NMDA currents, thus insights into the role of GABAergic inhibition are limited.' This represents a recognized methodological limitation rather than a refutation of findings.

result: The nuanced effects observed at different rostro-caudal locations may suggest differences in the functional characteristics, phenotypes, and projections of cell populations at specific coordinates within the pFL. Future investigation is needed to determine whether phenotypic and electrical properties of neurons at more rostral positions share the same identity as those at more caudal positions.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a fundamental concern about interpretation: 'Increasing the excitability of neurons provides little insights into the activity pattern and function of the activated neurons. Without recording from the activated neurons, it is impossible to know whether an effect on active expiration or any other respiratory phase is caused by bicuculline acting on rhythmogenic neurons or tonic neurons that modulate respiration.' This indicates that while the functional differences are observed, the mechanistic interpretation regarding distinct cell populations remains uncertain without additional cellular-level data.

result: The results highlight the functional diversity of the lateral parafacial region and emphasize the strong role of the most rostral locations in generating active expiration. The novel multidimensional map advanced understanding of the parafacial region and will enhance understanding of the expiratory oscillator's role in respiratory control, providing a foundation for future investigations into modulation, plasticity, and potential therapeutic targets.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Results from these experiments will be of value to those interested in the neural control of breathing and other neuroscientists as a framework for how to perform pharmacological mapping experiments in the future.' Reviewer 2 concludes 'Collectively, these findings advance our understanding of the presumed expiratory oscillator, the pFL, and highlight the functional heterogeneity in the functional response of this anatomical structure.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The study indicates that the rostro-caudal organization of the pFL and its influence on breathing is not simple and uniform,' affirming the significance of the findings despite methodological limitations.
